# Visual and Animation Production Pipeline

**D:** High-resolution pre-rendered 2D drawn with PixiJS; reference art, portraits and animation strips delivered as images and imported into a sprite manifest; one base and one upgrade per creature ([DEC-23](../DECISIONS_v0_3.md), 2D presentation migration of 2026-10-03).  
**P:** This production method, visual direction, budgets and acceptance gates. No images, strips, music or runtime code are generated by this document. The live production queue is `GPT6_2D_CONTENT_GENERATION.md` at the repository root (regenerated by `npm run sprites:queue`).

## 1. Visual goal

Aim for a readable mythological miniature world: strong silhouettes, expressive creatures, painted terrain, warm stone and bronze, purposeful cloth accents, and atmospheric lighting. Detail should reward the unit viewer without making battle stacks difficult to distinguish at gameplay zoom. Preserve the parchment/stone/navy/gold direction of the early boards as a proposed interface palette, not a requirement to copy their ornament or illegible text.

The initial Greek kit should look like one art direction across humans, monsters, buildings, props, portraits and UI. The finish is modern high-resolution pre-rendered 2D fantasy strategy art, not pixel art, flat vector or a photograph. The game is inspired by mythological strategy, not a reproduction of Heroes III or Age of Mythology assets. Do not extract their images, sprites, music, animations, icons or biographies. Record provenance and permission for every external asset used.

## 2. What generation means

Image generation is the intended production route for reference views, portraits, animation strips, painted backgrounds and effects (GPT-6 deliveries named by the production queue). An attractive image is **not** automatically a usable strip: every frame must keep the same scale, baseline, anatomy, equipment, colours and lighting; the strip must have an exact frame grid, a transparent background and padding so nothing touches the frame edge; and the action shown must exist in the creature's gameplay definition. Stock or hand-painted art, if used, passes the same checks, licensing and runtime import.

Choose one approved design per family before making its many derivatives. Do not independently generate sixteen unrelated creature images and ask the developer to turn them into a coherent army. Generate the base form first and derive the upgrade from it with explicit upgrade additions. The final runtime never calls a generation service.

## 3. Asset packet required before authoring

Every asset gets an ID, role, screen usage, scale reference, base/upgrade relationship if applicable, required views, frame size and anchor, animation strips, footprint policy, budget, accessible description and source/provenance record. Creature packets are in the [paired creature bible](03_creature_pairs_and_animation_bible.md). Non-creature coverage is in the [element inventory](04_environment_towns_ui_and_audio.md).

Use a neutral reference frame: a 512 x 512 frame with the baseline at 90 % of its height, a person-sized silhouette about 290 px tall, and one/two-hex footprint guides at one hex width = 240 px, seen from the fixed battle camera (about 20 degrees above the horizon). Check silhouette and proportions against this frame before spending time on surface detail. This is a presentation reference, not a change to logical unit scale or reach.

## 4. End-to-end creature workflow

### Gate A - Design the pair

Produce a shared design sheet for the pair at the same scale, first in grayscale silhouette, then in colour blocks. Lock anatomy and equipment placement across views. Add a labeled upgrade-delta panel rather than redesigning the species. The upgrade must read through at least one silhouette/equipment difference and one material/detail difference; color alone is not sufficient.

Approve the pair in a small battlefield montage as well as close-up. If the Hoplite's upgrade looks like a different faction or the Griffin's plume obscures its count label, revise now. Preserve a source-status note separating historical/mythological inspiration from original game design.

### Gate B - Canonical reference views

Deliver the canonical reference for each form: a three-quarter master view facing right (side, front and top views optional), transparent background, from the fixed battle camera, in `assets-source/creatures/reference/` (`creature.<pantheon>.tier<N>.<form>.ref.threequarter.png`). Repair intersecting limbs, fused equipment, extra or missing limbs, asymmetry errors and implausible joints in the reference before any strip is generated; every later image copies this design.

The reference is the design authority for its strips and portrait. Where a pantheon board and the written brief disagree on looks, follow the board; where they disagree on what the creature does, follow the gameplay definition.

### Gate C - Portraits and colour treatment

Each form gets its own portrait (`assets-source/icons/final/creature.<…>.portrait.png`, registered by `npm run icons:import`) painted from the approved reference, even when the two forms share most of their look. Use a consistent palette and material vocabulary (stone, bronze, linen, feathers) across the kit; check the imported runtime image, not just the delivered source.

Keep feather/cloth edges clean against transparency; avoid semi-transparent haze that turns into a halo on the battlefield. Team identity is a separate accent, banner or renderer tint and must not overwrite the family or upgrade identity.

### Gate D - One motion design, both forms

Generate each base-form strip first. Generate the upgraded form's same strip with the base strip attached, keeping every frame's pose, timing, camera, scale and baseline, so both forms share one motion design. Both forms use the same frame size, frame count, anchor and animation names. Upgraded equipment appears in every frame of every strip.

No attachment points are needed: a projectile leaves from a presentation origin point on the figure at the release moment and is drawn as its own sprite. Do not draw a projectile, a second weapon or an ability effect into a strip to imply a mechanic the creature does not have.

### Gate E - Animate and test mechanics alignment

Draw locomotion in place. The presentation system moves the sprite along a prevalidated path; it does not derive movement distance from the drawing. Attacks have anticipation, contact/release and recovery, but do not include rule effects not present in the unit definition. A magical-looking Temple Adept bolt remains that unit's ordinary ranged attack, not a second mana spell.

Each form's animations are drawn together on one sheet (one row per animation, six cells per row; `defend`+`hit` and `takeoff`+`landing` share a row), and the frame counts and rates put them inside the targets below: idle 6 frames at 3 fps (2 s), move 6 at 8 fps, attack and shoot 6 at 6 fps (1 s), defend 3 at 8 fps, hit 3 at 10 fps, death 6 at 5 fps with the last frame held, victory 6 at 4 fps (1.5 s), takeoff and landing 3 at 8 fps, fly 6 at 10 fps. Art-timing targets: idle 2-4 seconds, locomotion 0.7-1.3 seconds per cycle, attack/shoot 0.8-1.4 seconds, hit 0.2-0.45 seconds, death 1-1.8 seconds, victory 1.5-2.5 seconds. These are art-timing targets, not combat durations or simulator ticks.

Test baseline stability (no jitter or sliding feet between frames), hand grip, wing and weapon clearance inside the frame padding, lance/armor continuity, balance, and base/upgrade frame-for-frame correspondence. The first and last frames of a loop must join. Death is a non-looping strip; it never autoplays in the bestiary. A defend pose must remain distinguishable from attack anticipation.

### Gate F - Import and validate

Deliver each form's sheet to `assets-source/sprites/sheets/` under the exact name from the production queue (`sheet.creature.<form>.png`) and run `npm run sprites:cut`, which cuts it into one strip per animation (`sprite.creature.<form>.<animation>.png`, re-aligned on the creature's feet, with a preview to review), then `npm run sprites:import`. A single strip may also be delivered directly under its strip name. The importer checks transparency, the frame grid and the size, writes WebP under `assets-runtime/sprites/final/`, and flips the manifest entry from `placeholder` to `final`; no code changes are needed. Keep the delivered source files and the import output.

The importer validates format, grid and size; it does not establish good motion or art quality. Also inspect every required strip in the game, in battle and in the S18 viewer, at gameplay zoom and under each graphics quality preset.

### Gate G - Integrate all game contexts

Bind the sprite set to its existing creature ID, not its display name. Paint the portrait and army icon from the approved reference in a shared style and lighting. Verify battle, map guard marker, recruitment, hero army, comparison, and full bestiary usage. Confirm the upgraded unit has the right ID, strips, statistics and rank badge in each context.

Test missing texture, missing optional strip, interrupted load, fast view switching and reduced motion. A required asset missing in a production build fails content validation. A development placeholder remains usable and is labeled `placeholder` in the manifest, never silently presented as finished art.

## 5. Frames, anchors and scale

The renderer places every sprite by its explicit anchor, never by its image size. Every strip is authored facing right; the renderer mirrors enemies/defenders and westward map movement. Delivery conventions:

| Asset class | Delivery frame | Anchor (fraction of the frame) | Scale reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One-hex battle creature | 512 x 512 | Feet at 90 % of the height, horizontally centred | One hex width = 240 px |
| Two-hex battle creature | 768 x 512 | Feet at 90 %, centred over the two occupied cells | One hex width = 240 px |
| Mounted map hero | 320 x 320 | Ground point between the mount's feet at 88 %, centred | One map hex width = 150 px |
| Map site | 512 x 512 still | Ground contact at 92 %, centred | One map hex width = 280 px |
| Map decoration | 256 x 256 still | Ground contact at 95 %, centred | One map hex width = 280 px |
| Battle obstacle | 512 x 512 still | Ground at 92 %, centred | One hex width = 240 px |
| Siege piece | 512 x 512 still (keep 768 x 768) | Ground at 95 %, centred | One hex width = 240 px |
| Projectile | 128 x 32 still, pointing right | Centred | One hex width = 240 px |
| Effect | 256 x 256 frames | Centred at 62 % of the height | One hex width = 240 px |

A strip may be delivered at any uniform frame size from half to twice the target with the same shape; the importer scales the hex-width convention with it and reduces every delivery to its runtime size (half the delivery size for creatures, so a 512 x 512 frame becomes 256 x 256 at 120 px per hex). An optional sidecar JSON next to a delivery may override its frame rate, loop policy or anchor. Both boards use pointy-top hexes with a vertical foreshortening; the screen-to-hex transform (`packages/presentation/src/hexmath.ts`) is the only one, and picking never depends on sprite size.

The logical footprint belongs to the rules: one or two cells. The anchor centres a two-cell creature over its actual footprint, but it must not move its hit-test target or enlarge melee range. Huge wings may overhang graphically; unit selection and legal landing still use the explicit occupied cells. A flying form keeps the same ground anchor and is drawn at a presentation altitude above it.

## 6. Starting budgets to measure

| Asset class | Strips | Other starting limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary ground creature | 7 (`idle, move, attack, defend, hit, death, victory`) | 4-8 frames per strip at the delivery frame size |
| Shooter | 8 (adds `shoot`) | One projectile sprite per projectile kind, shared |
| Flier | 10 (adds `takeoff, fly, landing`) | Wings stay inside the frame padding |
| Active ability | +1 (`ability`) | Only for a declared active ability |
| Mounted map hero | `idle`, `walk` | Optional 8 directions; one direction is mirrored for the west |
| Map site / decoration | 1 still | Shared decoration sprites, thinned by the Low preset |

Texture memory, not file size, is the budget: an 8-frame strip of 256 x 256 runtime frames occupies about 2 MiB of texture memory once decoded (8 MiB if kept at the 512 x 512 delivery size). Load the sprite sets of the stacks actually present, release them on exit, and measure. The graphics presets (Low/Medium/High) change render resolution, decoration density, ambient motion, effects and frame cap; they never change a unit's silhouette or hide gameplay state. These are not universal limits or measured results.

Represent each stack with one animated figure plus its exact count label; a bounded formation of extra figures is an optional later proposal. Fifty Hoplites never require fifty independently animated sprites. Phase-offset cosmetic idles use a separate presentation seed.

Cache shared textures and pool transient projectiles/effects. Each figure keeps its own frame clock: loops run on the frame clock, one-shots on the tween clock, so skip/instant playback finishes them at once. Measure the complete fourteen-stack battlefield and repeated bestiary visits.

## 7. Animation manifest contract

The sprite manifest (`assets-runtime/sprites/manifest.json`, schema `pantheon-realms-sprites-1`) has the sections `creatures`, `heroes`, `sites`, `decor`, `obstacles`, `siege`, `projectiles` and `effects`. A creature entry records its status, provenance, facing, scale and one horizontal strip per animation with frame grid, frame rate, loop policy and explicit anchor. Values below are an example shape (abridged: a real Griffin set also has `move`, `defend` and `landing`), not a claim that the asset exists.

```json
{
  "griffin": {
    "status": "final",
    "provenance": "GPT-6 animation strips (GPT6_2D_CONTENT_GENERATION.md), imported by `npm run sprites:import`.",
    "facing": "right",
    "pixelsPerHex": 120,
    "animations": {
      "idle":    {"file": "sprites/final/creatures/griffin/idle.webp",    "frames": 6, "frameWidth": 384, "frameHeight": 256, "fps": 6,  "loop": true,  "anchor": [0.5, 0.9]},
      "takeoff": {"file": "sprites/final/creatures/griffin/takeoff.webp", "frames": 6, "frameWidth": 384, "frameHeight": 256, "fps": 10, "loop": false, "anchor": [0.5, 0.9]},
      "fly":     {"file": "sprites/final/creatures/griffin/fly.webp",     "frames": 8, "frameWidth": 384, "frameHeight": 256, "fps": 10, "loop": true,  "anchor": [0.5, 0.9]},
      "attack":  {"file": "sprites/final/creatures/griffin/attack.webp",  "frames": 8, "frameWidth": 384, "frameHeight": 256, "fps": 12, "loop": false, "anchor": [0.5, 0.9]},
      "hit":     {"file": "sprites/final/creatures/griffin/hit.webp",     "frames": 4, "frameWidth": 384, "frameHeight": 256, "fps": 12, "loop": false, "anchor": [0.5, 0.9]},
      "death":   {"file": "sprites/final/creatures/griffin/death.webp",   "frames": 8, "frameWidth": 384, "frameHeight": 256, "fps": 10, "loop": false, "anchor": [0.5, 0.9]},
      "victory": {"file": "sprites/final/creatures/griffin/victory.webp", "frames": 8, "frameWidth": 384, "frameHeight": 256, "fps": 8,  "loop": true,  "anchor": [0.5, 0.9]}
    }
  }
}
```

Animation vocabulary: base `idle, move, attack, defend, hit, death, victory`; plus `shoot` (shooters), `takeoff, fly, landing` (Flight) and `ability` (an active ability). `cast` is reserved for heroes; creatures do not cast. Required strip sets are family-specific and follow the gameplay definition (`requiredAnimations`). A missing optional animation falls back along a fixed chain (`shoot -> attack -> idle`, `fly -> move -> idle`, `ability -> attack -> idle`, ...); a missing death strip is presented by laying the figure down. The viewer enables a state selector only for strips that resolve.

## 8. Runtime playback state machine

An idle figure can enter a queued move (or takeoff, fly and landing), turn (horizontal mirroring), attack, shoot, ability, hit, defend, death or victory presentation. Transitions are driven by immutable rules events. Retaliation is a separate response event, not automatically triggered by the visible hit animation. Projectiles are cosmetic and use the resolved target; a drawn miss cannot undo resolved damage.

Presentation cues synchronize sound/flash with the known result. Use event ID deduplication so skipping an attack does not play its impact again later. Interrupting/cancelling playback snaps the presentation to the current authoritative state. Defeated figures cannot keep receiving queued attacks; dispose or cancel stale events by revision and actor ID.

Settings: 1x, 2x and Instant combat; manual bestiary playback at 0.5x/1x/2x; Pause/Stop/Restart; no rotation control (strips face right and are mirrored); no forced camera shake. Reduced motion disables idle autoplay, camera sway and pulsing backgrounds and shows a still frame. An explicit user-requested animation can play once with an immediate Stop control. The prior [behavior contract](../content/02_animation_behavior_contract.md) remains the interaction baseline.

## 9. File organization and review status

```text
assets-source/creatures/reference/      # canonical reference views per form
assets-source/icons/final/              # creature portraits (npm run icons:import)
assets-source/sprites/final/            # GPT-6 deliveries, named by the production queue
assets-source/sprites/content-plan.json # content plan (npm run sprites:plan)
assets-runtime/sprites/manifest.json    # sprite manifest (placeholder | final per entry)
assets-runtime/sprites/creatures/...    # labelled placeholders (npm run sprites:placeholders)
assets-runtime/sprites/final/...        # imported WebP strips (npm run sprites:import)
```

Use asset states `briefed -> reference_approved -> portrait_delivered -> strips_delivered -> imported -> integrated -> verified`; the runtime manifest records only `placeholder` or `final`. A file's existence is not verification. Store creator/source/license, generation or tool version, content version, hashes and review owner. Never place license keys, service credentials, or personal source material in a public asset packet.

## 10. Practical production order

Finish the Hoplite pair end to end first; then Peltast, Cavalry and Griffin pairs to prove humanoid, ranged, mounted and flight strip sets. Complete Temple Adept/Seer, Centaur/Sentinel, Minotaur/Warden, and Cyclops/Stormforged after those sets work. Within a form, deliver in queue order: reference (group A), portrait (B), battle strips (C). Build map heroes, map objects, battlefields, obstacles, effects and UI in parallel from their own briefs (groups D-H), not by inventing new unit definitions.

A polished complete pair is more informative than sixteen disconnected images. The campaign release still requires the complete pairs for every family it contains. Do not commission only the base units and treat upgrades as a last-minute color filter.
